"You," it says, "I order executed because you were condemned to death. You, because you caused your friend's condemnation. And you, because you disobeyed your general when ordered to kill him." He found a way to charge them with three crimes because he couldn't find any real crime in them.
original_excerpt: Hereupon the centurion in charge of the execution bade the guardsman sheathe his sword, and led the condemned man back to Piso, to restore to him the innocence which Fortune had restored to the soldier. They were led into his presence by their fellow soldiers amid the great joy of the whole camp, embracing one another and accompanied by a vast crowd. Piso mounted the tribunal in a fury and ordered them both to be executed, both him who had not murdered and him who had not been slain. What could be more unworthy than this? Because one was proved to be innocent, two perished. Piso even added a third: for he actually ordered the centurion, who had brought back the condemned man, to be put to death. Three men were set up to die in the same place because one was innocent. O, how clever is anger at inventing reasons for its frenzy! “You,” it says, “I order to be executed, because you have been condemned to death: you, because you have been the cause of your comrade’s condemnation, and you, because when ordered to put him to death you disobeyed your general.” He discovered the means of charging them with three crimes, because he could find no crime in them.

plain_english: Anger, I'm telling you, has a major flaw — it hates being controlled. It gets furious at the truth itself when it comes out against its wishes. It attacks its victims with shouting, wild noise, and wild gestures of the whole body, along with insults and curses. Reason doesn't act this way. When reason must destroy, it quietly and calmly wipes out entire households. It destroys whole families of enemies of the state, along with their wives and children. It tears down their homes, levels them to the ground, and erases the names of those who are enemies of freedom. It does this without grinding its teeth or shaking its head, or doing anything unfit for a judge. A judge's face should be especially calm and composed when pronouncing an important sentence. "Why do you need to bite your own lips when you want to hit someone?" asks Hieronymus. What would he have said if he had seen a governor leap down from his platform, grab the ceremonial rods from his attendant, and tear his own clothes because others weren't being torn fast enough for his liking? Why do you need to overturn the table, throw down the cups, bang yourself against the columns, tear your hair, and beat your thigh and chest? How violent do you think anger must be if it turns back on itself this way, just because it can't strike out at others as fast as it wants? People like this have to be held back by bystanders and begged to make peace with themselves. But someone who assigns each person the punishment they deserve while free from anger — he does none of these things.
original_excerpt: Irascibility, I say, has this fault—it is loth to be ruled: it is angry with the truth itself, if it comes to light against its will: it assails those whom it has marked for its victims with shouting and riotous noise and gesticulation of the entire body, together with reproaches and curses. Not thus does reason act: but if it must be so, she silently and quietly wipes out whole households, destroys entire families of the enemies of the state, together with their wives and children, throws down their very dwellings, levels them with the ground, and roots out the names of those who are the foes of liberty. This she does without grinding her teeth or shaking her head, or doing anything unbecoming to a judge, whose countenance ought to be especially calm and composed at the time when he is pronouncing an important sentence. “What need is there,” asks Hieronymus, “for you to bite your own lips when you want to strike some one?” What would he have said, had he seen a proconsul leap down from the tribunal, snatch the fasces from the lictor, and tear his own clothes because those of others were not torn as fast as he wished. Why need you upset the table, throw down the drinking cups, knock yourself against the columns, tear your hair, smite your thigh and your breast? How vehement do you suppose anger to be, if it thus turns back upon itself, because it cannot find vent on another as fast as it wishes? Such men, therefore, are held back by the bystanders and are begged to become reconciled with themselves. But he who while free from anger assigns to each man the penalty which he deserves, does none of these things.

plain_english: He often lets a person go free even after catching them in a crime. He does this if their regret seems genuine and suggests they'll do better in the future. He looks to see if their bad behavior runs deep or is just surface-level, as people say. He'll grant mercy when it won't harm either the criminal or society. Sometimes he'll punish major crimes more gently than minor ones. This happens when the big crime was a moment of poor judgment rather than cruelty, while the small crime showed hidden, sneaky, long-practiced deception. When two different people commit the same wrong, he won't give them the same punishment. One might have acted carelessly, while the other planned to cause harm.
original_excerpt: He often lets a man go after detecting his crime, if his penitence for what he has done gives good hope for the future, if he perceives that the man’s wickedness is not deeply rooted in his mind, but is only, as the saying is, skin-deep. He will grant impunity in cases where it will hurt neither the receiver nor the giver. In some cases he will punish great crimes more leniently than lesser ones, if the former were the result of momentary impulse, not of cruelty, while the latter were instinct with secret, underhand, long-practised craftiness. The same fault, committed by two separate men, will not be visited by him with the same penalty, if the one was guilty of it through carelessness, the other with a premeditated intention of doing mischief.

plain_english: When dealing with criminals, he will remember that punishment has two purposes: to reform bad people or to remove them permanently. Either way, he focuses on the future, not the past. As Plato said, "No wise person punishes someone because they sinned, but so they won't sin again. The past cannot be undone, but the future can be changed." When he makes public examples of criminals to show that wickedness doesn't pay, he executes them not just to end their lives, but so their deaths will stop others from following the same path. You can see how calm and clearheaded someone must be to weigh all these factors when handling the ultimate responsibility — the power over life and death. Justice wielded by an angry person is dangerous.
original_excerpt: In all dealing with crime he will remember that the one form of punishment is meant to make bad men better, and the other to put them out of the way. In either case he will look to the future, not to the past: for, as Plato says, “no wise man punishes any one because he has sinned, but that he may sin no more: for what is past cannot be recalled, but what is to come may be checked.” Those, too, whom he wishes to make examples of the ill success of wickedness, he executes publicly, not merely in order that they themselves may die, but that by dying they may deter others from doing likewise. You see how free from any mental disturbance a man ought to be who has to weigh and consider all this, when he deals with a matter which ought to be handled with the utmost care, I mean, the power of life and death. The sword of justice is ill-placed in the hands of an angry man.

plain_english: Don't believe that anger makes you brave or noble. What it gives you isn't true courage — it's just empty pride. When disease makes a body swell up with bad fluids, that's not healthy growth. It's just bloating. People who go crazy and think they're above everyone else believe they have deep, inspiring thoughts. But there's nothing solid underneath. What you build without a foundation will collapse. Anger has no foundation either. It doesn't come from anything firm or lasting. It's just windy and empty — as different from true courage as recklessness is from bravery, or bragging is from real confidence, or cruelty is from being strict. There's a huge difference between a noble mind and an arrogant one. Anger never creates anything great or beautiful. Being constantly irritated seems like the mark of a weak, miserable mind that knows it's feeble. It's like people with diseased, sore-covered bodies who scream at the slightest touch. Anger mostly affects women and children. "But it affects men too." Yes, because many men have the minds of women or children. "But what about this — don't angry men sometimes say things that seem to come from greatness?" Sure, they do — but only to people who don't know what real greatness looks like. Take that disgusting, hateful saying: "Let them hate me, as long as they fear me." You can bet that was written in Sulla's time. I don't know which was worse — that he wanted to be hated or that he wanted to be feared.
original_excerpt: Neither ought it to be believed that anger contributes anything to magnanimity: what it gives is not magnanimity but vain glory. The increase which disease produces in bodies swollen with morbid humours is not healthy growth, but bloated corpulence. All those whose madness raises them above human considerations, believe themselves to be inspired with high and sublime ideas; but there is no solid ground beneath, and what is built without foundation is liable to collapse in ruin. Anger has no ground to stand upon, and does not rise from a firm and enduring foundation, but is a windy, empty quality, as far removed from true magnanimity as fool-hardiness from courage, boastfulness from confidence, gloom from austerity, cruelty from strictness. There is, I say, a great difference between a lofty and a proud mind: anger brings about nothing grand or beautiful. On the other hand, to be constantly irritated seems to me to be the part of a languid and unhappy mind, conscious of its own feebleness, like folk with diseased bodies covered with sores, who cry out at the lightest touch. Anger, therefore, is a vice which for the most part affects women and children. “Yet it affects men also.” Because many men, too, have womanish or childish intellects. “But what are we to say? do not some words fall from angry men which appear to flow from a great mind?” Yes, to those who know not what true greatness is: as, for example, that foul and hateful saying, “Let them hate me, provided they fear me,” which you may be sure was written in Sulla’s time. I know not which was the worse of the two things he wished for, that he might be hated or that he might be feared.

plain_english: He realizes that someday people will curse him, plot against him, and destroy him. What prayer does he add to this? May all the gods curse him — for finding a cure for hate so worthy of hatred. "Let them hate." How? "As long as they obey me?" No! "As long as they approve of me?" No! How then? "As long as they fear me!" I wouldn't even want to be loved on those terms. Do you think this was a brave saying? You're wrong. This isn't greatness — it's monstrous. You shouldn't believe the words of angry men. Their speech is loud and threatening, but their minds are as cowardly as possible. And don't suppose that even the most eloquent writer, Titus Livius, was right when he described someone as having "a great rather than a good character." These things can't be separated. A person must either be good or he can't be great. True greatness of mind means it stays unshaken, sound all through, firm and consistent to its very core. This can't exist in evil people. Evil people may be terrible, frantic, and destructive, but they can't have greatness. Greatness rests on goodness and gets its strength from it. "But through their words, actions, and outward show, they'll make you think they're great." True, they'll say something that might seem to show a great spirit — like Gaius Caesar. When he got angry at heaven for interfering with his ballet dancers (whom he copied more carefully than he watched when they performed), and because thunder frightened his parties with poorly aimed noise, he challenged Jupiter to a fight to the death, shouting Homer's verse:
original_excerpt: It occurs to his mind that some day people will curse him, plot against him, crush him: what prayer does he add to this? May all the gods curse him—for discovering a cure for hate so worthy of it. “Let them hate.” How? “Provided they obey me?” No! “Provided they approve of me?” No! How then? “Provided they fear me!” I would not even be loved upon such terms. Do you imagine that this was a very spirited saying? You are wrong: this is not greatness, but monstrosity. You should not believe the words of angry men, whose speech is very loud and menacing, while their mind within them is as timid as possible: nor need you suppose that the most eloquent of men, Titus Livius, was right in describing somebody as being “of a great rather than a good disposition.” The things cannot be separated: he must either be good or else he cannot be great, because I take greatness of mind to mean that it is unshaken, sound throughout, firm and uniform to its very foundation; such as cannot exist in evil dispositions. Such dispositions may be terrible, frantic, and destructive, but cannot possess greatness; because greatness rests upon goodness, and owes its strength to it. “Yet by speech, action, and all outward show they will make one think them great.” True, they will say something which you may think shows a great spirit, like Gaius Caesar, who when angry with heaven because it interfered with his ballet-dancers, whom he imitated more carefully than he attended to them when they acted, and because it frightened his revels by its thunders, surely ill-directed,[9] challenged Jove to fight, and that to the death, shouting the Homeric verse:—

plain_english:
"Take me away, or I'll take you away!"

How insane was that! He must have believed either that not even Jupiter could hurt him, or that he could hurt Jupiter himself. I think this saying of his really motivated the conspirators. It seemed like the ultimate test of patience — having to put up with someone who wouldn't even put up with Jupiter.
original_excerpt:
“Carry me off, or I will carry thee!”

How great was his madness! He must have believed either that he could not be hurt even by Jupiter himself, or that he could hurt even Jupiter itself. I imagine that this saying of his had no small weight in nerving the minds of the conspirators for their task: for it seemed to be the height of endurance to bear one who could not bear Jupiter.

plain_english: There is nothing great or noble about anger, even when it seems powerful and looks down on both gods and men. Anyone who thinks anger creates greatness of mind might as well think luxury does too. Such a person wants to rest on ivory beds, wear purple clothes, and live under golden roofs. He wants to move mountains, dam up seas, change the course of rivers, and hang forests in mid-air. He would think greed shows greatness of mind too. The greedy man hoards piles of gold and silver. He treats entire provinces like fields on his personal estate. He puts more land under single managers than whole territories that consuls once governed. He would think lust shows greatness of mind as well. The lustful man swims across dangerous waters, castrates groups of boys, and puts himself within reach of angry husbands' swords — completely ignoring the risk of death. He would think ambition shows greatness of mind too. The ambitious man won't settle for holding office once a year. If he could, he would fill the entire calendar with his name alone and cover the whole world with his titles. It doesn't matter how far or high these passions reach — they are narrow, pitiful, and base. Only virtue is lofty and sublime. Nothing is truly great unless it is also peaceful.
original_excerpt: There is therefore nothing great or noble in anger, even when it seems to be powerful and to contemn both gods and men alike. Any one who thinks that anger produces greatness of mind, would think that luxury produces it: such a man wishes to rest on ivory, to be clothed with purple, and roofed with gold; to remove lands, embank seas, hasten the course of rivers, suspend woods in the air. He would think that avarice shows greatness of mind: for the avaricious man broods over heaps of gold and silver, treats whole provinces as merely fields on his estate, and has larger tracts of country under the charge of single bailiffs than those which consuls once drew lots to administer. He would think that lust shows greatness of mind: for the lustful man swims across straits, castrates troops of boys, and puts himself within reach of the swords of injured husbands with complete scorn of death. Ambition, too, he would think shows greatness of mind: for the ambitious man is not content with office once a year, but, if possible, would fill the calendar of dignities with his name alone, and cover the whole world with his titles. It matters nothing to what heights or lengths these passions may proceed: they are narrow, pitiable, grovelling. Virtue alone is lofty and sublime, nor is anything great which is not at the same time tranquil.
